title: The TFTP Protocol (Revision 2)
subtitle: A file-transfer protocol so small it fits in a boot ROM.
summary: TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, moves a file between two machines over UDP. It can only read or write one file at a time: no directory listings, no login. Each 512-byte block of data must be acknowledged before the next is sent, which keeps the code tiny. That simplicity is why diskless machines and network devices still use it to fetch boot images.

plainLanguage.summary: TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, moves a file between two machines over UDP. It can only read or write a file, with no directory listings and no login. Each 512-byte block must be acknowledged before the next is sent, which keeps the code very small. Diskless machines and network devices still use it to fetch boot images.

questions: why does network booting use tftp
what is the difference between tftp and ftp

tldr.problem: A machine with almost no software, such as a diskless workstation booting from ROM, still needs to fetch a file over the network.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a read or write request to UDP port 69, then the two sides exchange fixed 512-byte DATA blocks, each answered by an ACK carrying the same block number.
tldr.outcome: The whole protocol is five packet types and no authentication, so it fits in firmware, and it is still how many devices fetch boot images and configuration files.

today: TFTP is still widely used where a tiny, unauthenticated transfer is enough. The best-known case is network booting: PXE firmware asks a DHCP server for an address and a boot file name, then downloads that file with TFTP. Routers, switches, VoIP phones and other embedded devices also use it to load firmware and configuration, usually on a trusted management network. Because it has no authentication or encryption, it is rarely exposed to the open Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a very simple way to move files. The RFC says it was named for exactly that: it is "a simple protocol to transfer files, and therefore was named the Trivial File Transfer Protocol." It runs on top of the User Datagram Protocol (UDP, RFC 768), so it can move files between machines on different networks, although the RFC does not rule out other datagram protocols.

It is deliberately small. The only things it can do are read and write files (or mail) on a remote server. It cannot list directories, and it has no provisions for user authentication. Like other Internet protocols it passes 8-bit bytes.

This document, Revision 2, is an Internet Standard (STD 33) and obsoletes RFC 783. The author credits Noel Chiappa with the original design and with the May 1992 revision that fixed the "Sorcerer's Apprentice" bug.

The RFC defines three transfer modes: netascii, octet (raw 8-bit bytes) and mail. It states that mail mode is obsolete and should not be implemented or used.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP is a very simple protocol for moving files, which is why it is called Trivial. It runs over UDP and can only read and write files on a remote server. It cannot list directories and has no user authentication.

sections.title: Overview of the Protocol
sections.content:
Every transfer starts with a request to read or write a file, and that request also asks for a connection. If the server agrees, the file travels in fixed-length blocks of 512 bytes. Each DATA packet carries one block and must be answered by an acknowledgment (ACK) before the next one is sent. A DATA packet shorter than 512 bytes marks the end of the transfer.

If a packet is lost, the receiver times out and may retransmit its last packet, which prompts the sender to retransmit the lost one. The sender only has to keep one packet on hand, because the lock-step acknowledgment guarantees that all older ones arrived. Both machines are senders and receivers: one sends data and receives ACKs, the other sends ACKs and receives data.

The RFC admits this is restrictive on purpose. Fixed blocks make memory allocation straightforward, and lock-step acknowledgment gives flow control and removes any need to reorder incoming data.

One packet in flight
The sender waits for an ACK before sending the next block.
Timeouts, not NAKs
Lost packets are recovered by timing out and resending; the RFC gives no specific timeout value.
Short block means done
A block of 0 to 511 bytes ends the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer starts with a request to read or write a file. The file then moves in blocks of 512 bytes. Each DATA packet carries one block and must be acknowledged (ACK) before the next is sent. A DATA packet shorter than 512 bytes marks the end. If a packet is lost, the receiver times out and retransmits its last packet.

sections.title: Relation to Other Protocols
sections.content:
TFTP is designed to sit on UDP, which in turn sits on the Internet Protocol. A TFTP packet therefore has, in order, an optional local medium header, an Internet header, a UDP (the RFC says "Datagram") header and the TFTP header. TFTP does not specify any values in the Internet header.

It does use the UDP header. The source and destination port fields carry the transfer identifiers (TIDs), and the length field reflects the size of the TFTP packet. Because TIDs are handed to UDP as ports, they must be between 0 and 65,535.

The TFTP header itself is a 2-byte opcode that says which kind of packet follows (DATA, ERROR and so on). The appendix reprints the UDP header format for convenience and reminds implementers that TFTP need not run on UDP, and that a UDP checksum field containing zero means the checksum is unused.
sections.plainLanguage: A TFTP packet sits inside UDP, which sits inside IP. The UDP source and destination ports carry the transfer identifiers (TIDs), one for each end. The TFTP header itself begins with a 2-byte opcode that says which kind of packet follows.

sections.title: Initial Connection Protocol
sections.content:
A transfer begins when a client sends a write request (WRQ, to write onto a foreign file system) or a read request (RRQ, to read from it). The positive reply to a write request is an ACK, and the positive reply to a read request is the first DATA packet. An ERROR packet in reply means the request was denied.

Each end picks a transfer identifier (TID) for itself, to be used for the whole connection. They should be chosen randomly so that the same number is very unlikely to be picked twice in a row. The client sends its request from its own TID to the well-known port 69 (decimal; 105 octal) on the server. The server answers from a TID of its own to the client's TID, and from then on those two TIDs are used for the transfer.

Block numbers start at 1, so the ACK that accepts a write request carries block number 0. After the setup, each side checks that the source TID of every packet matches the agreed value. A packet from the wrong TID is discarded and an ERROR packet is sent to its source, without disturbing the real transfer.

The RFC gives an example: if a request is duplicated in the network, the server may create two connections with different TIDs. The client continues with the first response and rejects the second with an ERROR packet, and the first connection survives.
sections.plainLanguage: A client starts by sending a read request (RRQ) or write request (WRQ) to the server's well-known port 69. A write request is answered with an ACK, a read request with the first DATA packet, and a denied request with an ERROR packet. Each end picks its own random TID for the whole transfer.

sections.title: TFTP Packets
sections.content:
TFTP has five packet types, each starting with a 2-byte opcode: 1 for read request (RRQ), 2 for write request (WRQ), 3 for DATA, 4 for ACK and 5 for ERROR.

RRQ and WRQ carry a file name, a zero byte, a mode string and a final zero byte. The file name is netascii; the mode is "netascii", "octet" or "mail" in any mix of upper and lower case. DATA packets carry a 2-byte block number, starting at 1, followed by 0 to 512 bytes of data. ACK packets carry just the block number being acknowledged. ERROR packets carry a 2-byte error code and a zero-terminated message intended for humans.

The error codes are 0 (not defined, see message), 1 (file not found), 2 (access violation), 3 (disk full or allocation exceeded), 4 (illegal TFTP operation), 5 (unknown transfer ID), 6 (file already exists) and 7 (no such user).

Modes matter to the data. In netascii the receiver converts text to its own format; octet is for files in the sender's 8-bit format and a file sent and returned must come back identical. The RFC adds that other modes can be defined by cooperating hosts, but there is no central authority to assign them.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP has five packet types, each starting with a 2-byte opcode: read request, write request, DATA, ACK and ERROR. Requests carry a file name and a mode (netascii, octet or mail). DATA packets carry a block number starting at 1 and up to 512 bytes. ERROR packets carry a code and a message for people.

sections.title: Termination and Errors
sections.content:
A transfer ends normally with a DATA packet holding 0 to 511 bytes, which the RFC also describes as a datagram length under 516. It is acknowledged like every other DATA packet. The host sending the final ACK may close at once, but "dallying" is encouraged: it waits a while so it can resend the final ACK if the sender's last DATA packet arrives again, which shows the ACK was lost.

The host sending the last DATA must retransmit it until it is acknowledged or the sender times out. If it times out, the transfer may still have succeeded, or it may not; in any case the connection has closed.

Most errors end the connection. An ERROR packet is sent as a courtesy, but it is never acknowledged or retransmitted, so it may not arrive, and timeouts must detect that case. Errors come from requests that cannot be satisfied, packets that cannot be explained by delay or duplication, and loss of a resource such as disk space. The one error that does not end a transfer is a packet from the wrong source port.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer ends with a DATA packet of 0 to 511 bytes, acknowledged like any other. The host sending the final ACK may wait briefly before closing, in case that ACK was lost and the last DATA arrives again. The sender of the last DATA repeats it until acknowledged or until it times out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is brief. TFTP has no login or access control mechanism, so care must be taken over the rights given to a TFTP server process, to avoid exposing the server's file system. The RFC notes that TFTP is often installed so that only files with public read access are available and writing is disallowed.

In practice that means a TFTP server should expose a single directory of files you are happy for anyone on the network to read, and should refuse writes unless they are truly needed. There is no encryption either: file contents and names travel in the clear. These points come from the lack of any authentication in the protocol rather than from a flaw in a particular implementation.

The RFC itself says the protocol has "no provisions for user authentication." Anyone who can reach the server can send it a request.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP has no login or access control. A server should therefore expose only files that anyone may read, and should refuse writes unless truly needed. Nothing is encrypted, so file names and contents travel in the clear.

items.title: No authentication
items.text: There is no login; any host that can reach the server can ask for a file.

items.title: No directory listing
items.text: A client must already know the exact file name.

items.title: Access control is up to the server
items.text: The RFC suggests exposing only publicly readable files and disallowing writes.

items.title: Little flow or error machinery
items.text: Lock-step ACKs and timeouts replace windows, reordering and retransmission queues.
